arXiv:2606.01708v2 [cs.LG] 29 Sep 2026

Two-Fidelity Best-Action Identification
for Stochastic Minimax Tree

Peter Chen Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley Email: pllc@eecs.berkeley.edu    Xi Chen Affiliation: New York University Email: xc13@stern.nyu.edu
Abstract

We study fixed-confidence best-action identification (BAI) in stochastic minimax trees. This problem is increasingly relevant in modern AI planning, where deep minimax search and Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with language model long rollouts face a fundamental tradeoff: heuristic evaluations are cheap but biased, while accurate rollouts are reliable but prohibitively expensive. We propose 2FFS, a 2-fidelity minimax tree search paradigm that brings multi-fidelity flat bandit ideas into trees. 2FFS combines minimax-style fast expansion with MCTS-style stochastic sampling, adaptively deciding when to exploit cheap biased evaluations and when to invoke expensive accurate evaluations for local certification. We prove fixed-confidence correctness, establish finite stopping for exact identification, and give a polynomial-depth cost upper bound for general-depth trees. Guarantees are further extended to real-world multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). Across numerical stochastic-tree experiments, 2FFS uses substantially fewer samples and computational operations comparing to existing BAI-MCTS baseline11 1 Numerical implementation: https://github.com/PeterLauLukChen/2FFS.

1 Introduction

Modern decision-making systems often face a fundamental budget-allocation tradeoff: when reasoning over a large search space, should computation be used to expand the search tree more deeply, or to improve the reliability of the evaluations assigned to actions already under consideration? In two-player zero-sum planning and multi-agent reinforcement learning, this tradeoff is exemplified by the contrast between minimax-style tree search, which pushes depth using fast heuristic leaf evaluations, and Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), which allocates computation to repeated stochastic sampling and consequently grows a narrower, more selective tree.

A closely related tradeoff also arises in long-horizon reasoning and planning with large language models, where exhaustive tree expansion quickly becomes infeasible and each rollout, especially one involving a long chain-of-thought, can be costly. At a high level, this setting points to a common abstraction: a learner must allocate a limited sampling budget between cheap but biased information and expensive but accurate information. This viewpoint is closely connected to multi-fidelity bandits, in which an agent may query each arm at different fidelities, trading cost against accuracy in estimating its value. While the multi-fidelity multi-armed bandit (MF-MAB) literature [1, 2, 3, 4] formalizes this tradeoff in flat action spaces, and best-action identification in MCTS [5] studies fixed-confidence identification in minimax trees under a single stochastic oracle, the corresponding problem of multi-fidelity best-action identification in minimax trees remains largely unexplored.

In this work, we formalize this tradeoff in a minimax tree with two complementary sources of information: a fast oracle, which is cheap but biased, and a slow oracle, which is more costly but statistically accurate. The agent must adaptively allocate computation across the tree, deciding whether to expand the search using fast evaluations or to spend additional budget refining the values of nodes already on the frontier. Our objective is to identify the optimal root action under a fixed-confidence requirement while minimizing total evaluation cost. This exposes a principled crossover between α\alpha-β\beta-style expansion and MCTS-style sampling: at a frontier node, should the algorithm go one level deeper using the cheap biased fast oracle, or stay and reduce uncertainty using the expensive unbiased slow oracle?

Contributions.

Our work fills this gap by proposing 2FFS, a two-fidelity search algorithm for fixed-confidence best-action identification in stochastic minimax trees. 2FFS adaptively compares two routes at each decision-critical node: recursively expanding the tree using cheap biased fast evaluations, or locally certifying the node value using expensive but statistically accurate slow evaluations. On the theoretical side, we prove (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-PAC correctness and, for exact identification under a local regularity assumption, establish finite stopping together with a general-depth cost upper bound whose overhead is polynomial in the tree depth. The same exact-identification upper bound also gives a conservative bound for ε>0\varepsilon>0 runs, since the approximate stopping rule can only terminate earlier. To our knowledge, this is the first analytic framework for multi-fidelity bandits in a minimax-tree setting. Empirically, on synthetic stochastic minimax trees, we show that 2FFS substantially improves both sampling and computational efficiency compared with existing baseline.

Related works.

Viewed through the compute-allocation lens above, classical perfect-information two-player zero-sum search is dominated by minimax with α\alpha-β\beta pruning, where efficiency is driven by deeper expansion and pruning under deterministic leaf evaluation [6, 7]. MCTS takes the opposite perspective, treating action selection as an exploration–exploitation problem guided by bandit principles (UCB) and stochastic samples [8]. Empirical hybrids such as implicit minimax backups suggest these paradigms are complementary, but also echo classic game-tree pathology results: applying minimax to noisy point estimates can mis-rank moves as depth grows [9, 10]. On the theory side, BAI-MCTS formalizes root-action selection as fixed-confidence BAI in minimax trees with an unbiased sampling oracle [5]; in parallel, multi-fidelity bandits and Bayesian optimization study cost–accuracy tradeoffs between cheap biased approximations and expensive accurate evaluations [1, 11, 12, 2, 3, 4]. We defer further related works to Appendix A.

2 Problem Setup and Preliminaries

In this section, we formalize fixed-confidence BAI in two-fidelity stochastic minimax trees and introduces the notation used by the algorithm and analysis. We first define the tree model, the fast and slow oracles, and the frontier maintained by the learner. Then, we define local and propagated confidence intervals, the effective gaps that determine decision-relevant precision, and the recursive oracle complexity and dyadic scale surrogates used in the upper-bound proof.

2.1 Minimax tree with two-fidelity oracles

Stochastic minimax tree.

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a finite rooted tree with root rr and internal nodes alternating between Max and Min, with root rr as Max node. For each node v∈𝒯v\in\mathcal{T}, we denote Ch⁡(v)\mathrm{Ch}(v) as its set of children and d⁡(v)d(v) as its depth, and we define remaining depth of node vv as h⁡(v)≔D−d⁡(v)h(v)\coloneqq D-d(v), where DD is the depth of 𝒯\mathcal{T}. For notational simplicity, we assume the tree has balanced depth: a node vv is a leaf if and only if h⁡(v)=0h(v)=0.

Let ℒ\mathcal{L} be the set of leaves, and let each ℓ∈ℒ\ell\in\mathcal{L} have mean payoff μℓ\mu_{\ell}, then its minimax value V∗​(v)V^{*}(v) is defined by V∗​(ℓ)=μℓV^{*}(\ell)=\mu_{\ell}. For every internal node vv,

V∗​(v)={maxu∈Ch⁡(v)⁡V∗​(u),if ​v​ is a Max node,minu∈Ch⁡(v)⁡V∗​(u),if ​v​ is a Min node.V^{*}(v)=\begin{cases}\max_{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}V^{*}(u),&\text{if }v\text{ is a {Max} node},\\[4.0pt] \min_{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}V^{*}(u),&\text{if }v\text{ is a {Min} node}.\end{cases}

For each root action a∈Ch⁡(r)a\in\mathrm{Ch}(r), we write V∗​(r,a)≔V∗​(a)V^{*}(r,a)\coloneqq V^{*}(a). Thus, V∗​(⋅)V^{*}(\cdot) denotes node values, while V∗​(r,⋅)V^{*}(r,\cdot) denotes root-action values. We assume throughout that |Ch⁡(r)|≥2|\mathrm{Ch}(r)|\geq 2, so the BAI problem is nontrivial, and that the optimal root action is unique, which is given by a∗∈arg⁡maxa∈Ch⁡(r)​V∗​(r,a)a^{*}\in\arg\max_{a\in\mathrm{Ch}(r)}V^{*}(r,a), along with the root gap Δ∗≔V∗​(r,a∗)−maxa≠a∗⁡V∗​(r,a)\Delta_{*}\coloneqq V^{*}(r,a^{*})-\max_{a\neq a^{*}}V^{*}(r,a).

Definition 2.1 (Frontier).

A frontier ℱ⊆𝒯∖{r}\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\setminus\{r\} is a complete cut of the tree, meaning that every root-to-leaf path intersects ℱ\mathcal{F} in exactly one node.

At each round tt, the algorithm has an explored subtree 𝒯t⊆𝒯\mathcal{T}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{T} containing the root. A node becomes exposed when it first enters 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t}. The current frontier ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} consists of the exposed nodes at which recursive expansion has not yet proceeded; it forms a complete cut of the full tree. Expanding an exposed internal node reveals all of its children, queries the fast oracle at those children, and replaces the node by its children in the frontier. Any local slow samples already collected at the expanded node remain available for all future interval computations.

Two-fidelity node-wise evaluations.

Each exposed non-root node vv can be evaluated through two resources. In the multi-fidelity bandit viewpoint [1, 2, 4], querying an arm at fidelity mm produces a sample from a distribution νv,m\nu_{v,m} with mean μv,m\mu_{v,m} and known query cost λm\lambda_{m}. In our tree setting, the node vv plays the role of the arm, and we use two fidelities. The fast oracle (m=1)(m=1) is cheap and deterministic, but may be biased. The slow oracle (m=2)(m=2) is more expensive and stochastic, but unbiased for the true minimax value V∗​(v)V^{*}(v). Thus, the fast oracle provides a low-fidelity estimate and the slow oracle provides a high-fidelity estimate of the same node value.

Note that the fast-oracle bias is controlled by the remaining depth h⁡(v)h(v) through a known calibration envelope B:{0,…,D}→ℝ≥0B:\{0,\ldots,D\}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}, which satisfies

B⁡(0)=0,B⁡(h+1)≥B⁡(h)for every ​h∈{0,…,D−1},B(0)=0,\qquad B(h+1)\geq B(h)\quad\text{for every }h\in\{0,\ldots,D-1\}, (1)

We normalize query costs as λ1=1\lambda_{1}=1 and λ2=c≥1\lambda_{2}=c\geq 1. The two oracles are defined formally below.

Definition 2.2 (Fast oracle FF).

The fast oracle returns a deterministic value VF​(v)V_{F}(v). Equivalently, νv,1\nu_{v,1} is a degenerate distribution at VF​(v)V_{F}(v), so μv,1=VF​(v)\mu_{v,1}=V_{F}(v) and |VF​(v)−V∗​(v)|≤B⁡(h⁡(v)).|V_{F}(v)-V^{*}(v)|\leq B(h(v)).

Definition 2.3 (Slow oracle SS).

For each node vv, repeated slow-oracle queries return independent σ\sigma-sub-Gaussian samples Yv,sY_{v,s} with distribution νv,2\nu_{v,2} and mean μv,2=V∗​(v).\mu_{v,2}=V^{*}(v).

Remark 2.1.

The unbiased slow oracle setup is analogous to that of Kaufmann and Koolen [5], which defines the sampling oracle as mean-correct 𝔼⁡[Yl,s]=V∗​(l)\mathbb{E}[Y_{l,s}]=V^{*}(l); in §4, we instantiate it by adding actual noise to true minimax values. Also, unlike classical BAI-MCTS [5], where stochastic samples are attached to leaf rollouts, our slow oracle may be queried at any exposed non-root node. In §3.2, we add further worst-case guarantee to real-world applications, where slow-oracles are biased.

Remark 2.2 (Fast-oracle envelop).

We note that the envelope structure in Eq. (1) can be motivated by finite horizon MARL. Specifically, for a critic V^t\widehat{V}_{t} with the correct terminal value, discount 0≤γ≤10\leq\gamma\leq 1, and minimax Bellman residual ηt=∥V^t−𝒯t​V^t+1∥∞\eta_{t}=\lVert\widehat{V}_{t}-\mathcal{T}_{t}\widehat{V}_{t+1}\rVert_{\infty}, Bellman nonexpansiveness gives ∥V^t−Vt∗∥∞≤∑j=tH−1γj−t​ηj\lVert\widehat{V}_{t}-V_{t}^{*}\rVert_{\infty}\leq\sum_{j=t}^{H-1}\gamma^{j-t}\eta_{j}. A known bound ηj≤η¯\eta_{j}\leq\bar{\eta} provides the nondecreasing envelope B⁡(h)=η¯​∑i=0h−1γiB(h)=\bar{\eta}\sum_{i=0}^{h-1}\gamma^{i}.

2.2 Intervals, effective gaps, and recursive oracle complexity

In the fixed-confidence setting, a strategy adaptively chooses exposed nodes and query types, stops at a stopping time τ\tau, and outputs a recommended action a^τ∈Ch⁡(r)\hat{a}_{\tau}\in\mathrm{Ch}(r). Let NF​(τ)N^{F}(\tau) denote the total number of fast-oracle queries issued by time τ\tau, and let NvS​(τ)N_{v}^{S}(\tau) denote the number of slow-oracle queries issued at node vv. The total searching cost is

Cτ≔NF​(τ)+c​∑v∈𝒯NvS​(τ),C_{\tau}\coloneqq N^{F}(\tau)+c\sum_{v\in\mathcal{T}}N_{v}^{S}(\tau),

where cc is the slow-oracle cost λ2\lambda_{2}. Given (ε,δ)∈[0,∞)×(0,1)(\varepsilon,\delta)\!\in\![0,\infty)\!\times\!(0,1), we seek strategies that satisfy the (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-PAC guarantee: ℙ(τ<∞,V∗(r,a∗)−V∗(r,a^τ)>ε)≤δ\mathbb{P}\!\left(\tau<\infty,\ V^{*}(r,a^{*})\!-\!V^{*}(r,\hat{a}_{\tau})\!>\!\varepsilon\right)\!\leq\!\delta, while seeking low evaluation cost; our cost bounds hold with high probability.

We now introduce the interval objects used by 2FFS and the instance-dependent oracle complexity used in the upper bound. The construction has three layers: (i) local intervals combine the cheap fast evaluation with slow statistical evidence at the same node; (ii) propagated intervals carry child information upward through the minimax recursion; (iii) finally, we establish the ideal amount of oracle complexity needed to certify only the precision that can affect the root decision.

We first fix a feasible node-wise confidence allocation 𝜹=(δv)v∈𝒯∖{r}\boldsymbol{\delta}=(\delta_{v})_{v\in\mathcal{T}\setminus\{r\}}, which indicates that δv∈(0,1)\delta_{v}\in(0,1) and ∑v∈𝒯∖{r}δv≤δ\sum_{v\in\mathcal{T}\setminus\{r\}}\delta_{v}\leq\delta. For every exposed non-root node vv, the fast oracle gives the deterministic interval

IvF=[VF​(v)−B⁡(h⁡(v)),VF​(v)+B⁡(h⁡(v))].I_{v}^{F}=[V_{F}(v)-B(h(v)),\,V_{F}(v)+B(h(v))]. (2)

For slow samples, let V^v,n\widehat{V}_{v,n} be the empirical mean of the first nn slow-oracle samples at vv. Following from fixed-confidence bandit literature [13, 5, 14, 15, 2], we use the time-uniform radius βv​(⋅,δv)\beta_{v}(\cdot,\delta_{v}) satisfying

ℙ(∃n≥1:|V^v,n−V∗(v)|>βv(n,δv))≤δv,\mathbb{P}\left(\exists\,n\geq 1:\,\left|\widehat{V}_{v,n}-V^{*}(v)\right|>\beta_{v}(n,\delta_{v})\right)\leq\delta_{v}, (3)

where n↦βv​(n,δv)n\mapsto\beta_{v}(n,\delta_{v}) is non-increasing and βv​(n,δv)→0\beta_{v}(n,\delta_{v})\to 0 as n→∞n\to\infty. Let NvS​(t)N_{v}^{S}(t) be the number of slow queries issued at vv by round tt, the slow interval is then the running intersection

IvS​(t)={⋂j=1NvS​(t)[V^v,j−βv​(j,δv),V^v,j+βv​(j,δv)],NvS​(t)≥1,(−∞,+∞),NvS​(t)=0,I_{v}^{S}(t)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\bigcap_{j=1}^{N_{v}^{S}(t)}\left[\widehat{V}_{v,j}-\beta_{v}(j,\delta_{v}),\,\widehat{V}_{v,j}+\beta_{v}(j,\delta_{v})\right],&N_{v}^{S}(t)\geq 1,\\[10.0pt] (-\infty,+\infty),&N_{v}^{S}(t)=0,\end{cases} (4)

which further gives the direct local interval Ivloc​(t)≔IvF∩IvS​(t)I_{v}^{\mathrm{loc}}(t)\coloneqq I_{v}^{F}\cap I_{v}^{S}(t). Finally, we define the simultaneous-validity event by Eq. (5). Also, by Eq. (3) and the union bound, we always have ℙ⁡(ℰδ)≥1−δ\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{\delta})\geq 1-\delta.

ℰδ≔⋂v∈𝒯∖{r}⋂n≥1{|V^v,n−V∗(v)|≤βv(n,δv)}.\mathcal{E}_{\delta}\coloneqq\bigcap_{v\in\mathcal{T}\setminus\{r\}}\bigcap_{n\geq 1}\left\{\left|\widehat{V}_{v,n}-V^{*}(v)\right|\leq\beta_{v}(n,\delta_{v})\right\}. (5)
Propagated intervals.

If an internal node vv has been expanded, its children are exposed and carry effective intervals Iu​(t)=[Lu​(t),Uu​(t)]I_{u}(t)=[L_{u}(t),U_{u}(t)]. The child-backup interval is

Ivch​(t)={[maxu∈Ch⁡(v)⁡Lu​(t),maxu∈Ch⁡(v)⁡Uu​(t)],if ​v​ is a Max node,[minu∈Ch⁡(v)⁡Lu​(t),minu∈Ch⁡(v)⁡Uu​(t)],if ​v​ is a Min node.I_{v}^{\mathrm{ch}}(t)=\begin{cases}\left[\max_{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}L_{u}(t),\,\max_{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}U_{u}(t)\right],&\text{if }v\text{ is a {Max} node},\\[8.0pt] \left[\min_{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}L_{u}(t),\,\min_{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}U_{u}(t)\right],&\text{if }v\text{ is a {Min} node}.\end{cases} (6)

If vv is a leaf or not expanded yet, we set Ivch​(t)=(−∞,+∞)I_{v}^{\mathrm{ch}}(t)=(-\infty,+\infty). For every explored non-root node, the effective interval combines direct local evidence and descendant evidence: Iv​(t)=Ivloc​(t)∩Ivch​(t)I_{v}(t)=I_{v}^{\mathrm{loc}}(t)\cap I_{v}^{\mathrm{ch}}(t). We note that the minimax backup in Eq. (6) preserves validity and does not increase interval width. The following two lemmas formalize these properties; their proofs are given in Appendix B.2.

Lemma 2.3.

Fix a frontier ℱ\mathcal{F} and suppose that each frontier interval [Lv,Uv][L_{v},U_{v}], v∈ℱv\in\mathcal{F}, contains V∗​(v)V^{*}(v). Under the recursive backup in Eq. (6), (i) every ancestor uu of a frontier node satisfies V∗​(u)∈[Lu,Uu]V^{*}(u)\in[L_{u},U_{u}]; and (ii) if every frontier interval has half-width at most ww, then every propagated ancestor interval also has half-width at most ww.

Lemma 2.4 (Simultaneous interval validity).

On ℰδ\mathcal{E}_{\delta}, every effective interval constructed from Eqs. (2)–(6) is valid at every round tt. In particular, V∗​(v)∈Iv​(t)V^{*}(v)\in I_{v}(t) for every explored non-root node vv, and the intervals of root children and the root backup are valid as well.

Effective gap.

A node does not necessarily need to be estimated down to its own local sibling gap. The value of a node vv can affect the final recommendation only if its uncertainty propagates through every ancestor and changes the comparison between root actions. Along this path, any large value separation creates a bottleneck: once the uncertainty below vv is smaller than that separation, further refinement cannot change the root decision. We therefore define the effective gap of a node as the precision scale needed to certify that node for the purpose of root-action identification.

Definition 2.4 (Effective gap).

Set the root effective gap to Δreff≔Δ∗\Delta_{r}^{\mathrm{eff}}\coloneqq\Delta_{*}. For every non-root node vv, let p⁡(v)p(v) denotes the parent of vv, we define recursively

Δveff≔max⁡{Δp⁡(v)eff,|V∗​(v)−V∗​(p⁡(v))|}.\Delta_{v}^{\mathrm{eff}}\coloneqq\max\!\left\{\Delta_{p(v)}^{\mathrm{eff}},\,|V^{*}(v)-V^{*}(p(v))|\right\}.

Thus, Δveff\Delta_{v}^{\mathrm{eff}} records the largest bottleneck encountered on the path from the root to vv. If this quantity is large, then vv only needs to be estimated coarsely: Proposition B.10 shows that a call at scale kk requires Δveff≤2​ρk\Delta_{v}^{\mathrm{eff}}\leq 2\rho_{k}.

Reference recursive oracle complexity.

To derive cost guarantees, we first define an idealized reference oracle complexity H∗H^{*} under perfect gap information within our recursive certification model. Our main theorem shows that 2FFS, despite not knowing the effective gaps or the cheaper route in advance, has cost within a polynomial-depth factor of this ideal reference complexity.

For a target precision ρ>0\rho>0, we first define the local cost of certifying a single exposed node vv. Let

mv(ρ,δv)≔inf{n∈ℕ:n≥1,βv(n,δv)≤14ρ}.m_{v}(\rho,\delta_{v})\coloneqq\inf\!\left\{n\in\mathbb{N}:\,n\geq 1,\,\beta_{v}(n,\delta_{v})\leq\tfrac{1}{4}\rho\right\}.

After mv​(ρ,δv)m_{v}(\rho,\delta_{v}) slow samples, the slow confidence interval has width at most ρ/2\rho/2. The factor 1/41/4 is chosen so that either the fast interval alone, 2​B​(h⁡(v))≤ρ/22B(h(v))\leq\rho/2, or the slow confidence interval alone, 2​βv​(n,δv)≤ρ/22\beta_{v}(n,\delta_{v})\leq\rho/2, is sufficient to make the direct local interval IvlocI_{v}^{\mathrm{loc}} have width at most ρ/2\rho/2.

The corresponding local certification cost is

Γv​(ρ,δv)={0,if ​B​(h⁡(v))≤14​ρ,c⋅mv​(ρ,δv),if ​B​(h⁡(v))>14​ρ.\Gamma_{v}(\rho,\delta_{v})=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if }B(h(v))\leq\tfrac{1}{4}\rho,\\[3.0pt] c\cdot m_{v}(\rho,\delta_{v}),&\text{if }B(h(v))>\tfrac{1}{4}\rho.\end{cases} (7)

Thus, Γv​(ρ,δv)\Gamma_{v}(\rho,\delta_{v}) is the slow-oracle cost needed to certify the value of vv locally at precision ρ\rho, after vv has already been exposed. The first case means that the fast interval is already narrow enough, so no slow sample is needed at vv.

We now define the recursive subtree oracle complexity. For a fixed confidence allocation 𝜹\boldsymbol{\delta}, Jv∗​(𝜹)J_{v}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\delta}) is a reference cost for the subtree rooted at vv, using effective-gap information. At each internal node, it compares two routes: certify vv locally, or expand vv and add all child reference costs:

Jv∗​(𝜹)={Γv​(Δveff,δv),if ​h​(v)=0,min⁡{Γv​(Δveff,δv),|Ch⁡(v)|+∑u∈Ch⁡(v)Ju∗​(𝜹)},if ​h​(v)≥1.J_{v}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\delta})=\begin{cases}\Gamma_{v}(\Delta_{v}^{\mathrm{eff}},\delta_{v}),&\text{if }h(v)=0,\\[5.0pt] \min\!\left\{\Gamma_{v}(\Delta_{v}^{\mathrm{eff}},\delta_{v}),\,|\mathrm{Ch}(v)|+\sum_{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}J_{u}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\delta})\right\},&\text{if }h(v)\geq 1.\end{cases} (8)

This induces the root oracle complexity H⁡(𝜹)≔|Ch⁡(r)|+∑a∈Ch⁡(r)Ja∗​(𝜹)H(\boldsymbol{\delta})\coloneqq|\mathrm{Ch}(r)|+\sum_{a\in\mathrm{Ch}(r)}J_{a}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\delta}), where |Ch⁡(r)||\mathrm{Ch}(r)| is the cost of initially exposing all root actions, and gives us the optimized recursive oracle complexity H∗H^{*}:

H∗≔inf𝜹​feasibleH⁡(𝜹).H^{*}\coloneqq\inf_{\boldsymbol{\delta}\,\mathrm{feasible}}H(\boldsymbol{\delta}). (9)
Remark 2.5.

We note that instance-dependent complexity measures are standard in fixed-confidence BAI. Classical bounds are often stated in terms of gap-dependent hardness quantities such as H1=∑i≠i∗Δi−2H_{1}=\sum_{i\neq i^{*}}\Delta_{i}^{-2}, while refined analyses use information-theoretic characteristic times to quantify the intrinsic difficulty of an instance [16, 17, 18]. BAI-MCTS and multi-fidelity BAI follow the same convention, using tree- or fidelity-dependent oracle complexities to state adaptive cost guarantees [5, 2, 4]. Our H∗H^{*} serves as an analysis-only recursive oracle complexity under perfect gap information, rather than an information-theoretic lower bound; see Appendix B.8.

Dyadic scale surrogates.

Following from Remark 2.5, the algorithm does not know the effective gaps and therefore cannot target Jv∗​(𝜹)J_{v}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\delta}) directly. Instead, 2FFS works on a dyadic precision grid, which initializes by exposing the root children with fast queries, then sets

ρ0≔maxa∈Ch⁡(r)⁡(Ua​(0)−La​(0)),ρk+1≔12​ρk,k≥0.\rho_{0}\coloneqq\max_{a\in\mathrm{Ch}(r)}\bigl(U_{a}(0)-L_{a}(0)\bigr),\qquad\rho_{k+1}\coloneqq\tfrac{1}{2}\rho_{k},\qquad k\geq 0.

If ρ0=0\rho_{0}=0, the root-child values are already known exactly and the algorithm stops immediately; otherwise the following scales are used. A node vv is scale-kk safe at round tt if Uv​(t)−Lv​(t)≤12​ρkU_{v}(t)-L_{v}(t)\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\rho_{k}. The scale-kk local certification cost is Γv(k)​(δv)≔Γv​(ρk,δv)\Gamma_{v}^{(k)}(\delta_{v})\coloneqq\Gamma_{v}(\rho_{k},\delta_{v}), and the operational rules that decide which scale and which node to refine are given in Algorithm 1.

3 2FFS Tree Search: Two-Fidelity Fast-Slow Tree Search

2FFS maintains a confidence interval [Lv​(t),Uv​(t)][L_{v}(t),U_{v}(t)] for each exposed node and repeatedly certifies the root decision. At each round, the algorithm first checks whether some root action is already ε\varepsilon-optimal according to the current intervals. If not, it selects one decision-relevant side of one root child and calls a recursive resolver Resolve​(v,s,k)\textsc{Resolve}(v,s,k), where s∈{L,U}s\in\{L,U\} is the endpoint to certify and kk is the active dyadic scale. Figure 1 visualizes these three pieces: the root test, the recursive resolver, and the scale-kk child-selection rules.

At the root, let at∈argmaxa∈Ch⁡(r)La​(t)a_{t}\in\mathop{\rm argmax}_{a\in\mathrm{Ch}(r)}L_{a}(t) and bt∈argmaxa∈Ch⁡(r)∖{at}Ua​(t)b_{t}\in\mathop{\rm argmax}_{a\in\mathrm{Ch}(r)\setminus\{a_{t}\}}U_{a}(t) be the current leader and challenger. 2FFS stops once a root action is certified to be ε\varepsilon-optimal: La^t​(t)≥maxa≠a^t⁡Ua​(t)−εL_{\hat{a}_{t}}(t)\!\geq\!\max_{a\neq\hat{a}_{t}}U_{a}(t)-\varepsilon. If this test fails, the leader’s lower endpoint and the challenger’s unresolved endpoint information are the two quantities that can still change the root decision. 2FFS refines whichever of these two root-side certificates is currently coarser. For the leader this means the lower side LatL_{a_{t}}; for the challenger it means the coarsest unresolved side among LbtL_{b_{t}} and UbtU_{b_{t}}.

The call Resolve​(v,s,k)\textsc{Resolve}(v,s,k) tries to certify endpoint ss of node vv at scale ρk\rho_{k}. It has two competing routes. The local route takes slow samples directly at vv. The recursive route expands below vv, uses fast evaluations on the children, and continues recursively only along the currently relevant child. These routes remain available throughout the run: even after vv has been expanded, 2FFS may still take slow samples at vv. This local reversibility is important because the cheaper route is not known in advance. Recursive spending at node vv and scale kk is capped by 𝖡v,krec=αh⁡(v)​Γv(k)​(δv)\mathsf{B}_{v,k}^{\mathrm{rec}}=\alpha_{h(v)}\Gamma_{v}^{(k)}(\delta_{v}), and every child call uses a scale no finer than the parent scale kk. If the recursive route cannot make admissible progress within this budget, the resolver falls back to one slow local query at vv.

Inside an expanded node, the recursive route follows the live child rule in Figure 1 (right). In selector cases, the live child is the endpoint that currently determines the minimax backup. In comparison cases, 2FFS does not force all children to become fully certified. Instead, it lazily removes a child once the child is already outside the scale-kk comparison margin, or once the child has the required same-side certificate. Among the remaining live children, only the current endpoint-most blocker is refined recursively. The comparison rows use the following discharge margins. For a Max node on side LL, write λL​(v,t)=maxu⁡Lu​(t)\lambda_{L}(v,t)=\max_{u}L_{u}(t); a child is no longer live if

Uu​(t)≤λL​(v,t)+ρk/2or𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉L​(u,k,t).U_{u}(t)\leq\lambda_{L}(v,t)+\rho_{k}/2\quad\text{or}\quad\mathsf{Comp}_{L}(u,k,t).

For a Min node on side UU, write λU​(v,t)=minu⁡Uu​(t)\lambda_{U}(v,t)=\min_{u}U_{u}(t); a child is no longer live if

Lu​(t)≥λU​(v,t)−ρk/2or𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉U​(u,k,t).L_{u}(t)\geq\lambda_{U}(v,t)-\rho_{k}/2\quad\text{or}\quad\mathsf{Comp}_{U}(u,k,t).

The formal implementation maintains scale-local counters, monotone side flags 𝖣𝗈𝗇𝖾s​(v,k)\mathsf{Done}_{s}(v,k), observable certificates 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉s​(v,k,t)\mathsf{Comp}_{s}(v,k,t), and capped unresolved scales Ks≤k​(v,t)K_{s}^{\leq k}(v,t). These details are given in Appendix B.3, which are not needed to understand the main flow above but important for the proofs.

3.1 Theoretical results

We present three results: algorithmic correctness and a general-depth cost upper bound guarantee along with finite stopping time guarantee. First, we provide algorithm’s (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-PAC correctness:

Theorem 3.1 (PAC correctness).

Fix any feasible confidence allocation 𝛅=(δv)v∈𝒯∖{r}\boldsymbol{\delta}=(\delta_{v})_{v\in\mathcal{T}\setminus\{r\}} and any ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0. Consider Algorithm 1 run with accuracy ε\varepsilon, let τ\tau be its stopping time, and, on the event {τ<∞}\{\tau<\infty\}, let a^τ\hat{a}_{\tau} be the returned root child. Then, ℙ⁡(τ<∞​ and ​V∗​(r,a∗)−V∗​(r,a^τ)>ε)≤δ\mathbb{P}\!\left(\tau<\infty\text{ \emph{and} }V^{*}(r,a^{*})-V^{*}(r,\hat{a}_{\tau})>\varepsilon\right)\leq\delta. In fact, on the simultaneous-validity event ℰδ\mathcal{E}_{\delta}, every finite-time recommendation made by the stopping rule is ε\varepsilon-optimal.

Remark 3.2.

We note that Theorem 3.1 uses only simultaneous interval validity and the root stopping rule and does not use any assumptions in the later upper-bound proof. Its proof is very straightforward, and we defer it to Appendix B.4. The finite stopping guarantee is elaborated in Theorem 3.6.

Now, we move to establish the upper bound for cost using the reference oracle complexity H∗H^{*}. Before that, we first explicitly state several required regular assumptions along with their discussions.

Assumption 3.3 (Local dyadic scale regularity).

Fix the confidence allocation 𝛅\boldsymbol{\delta}, we assume there exist constants Λpre≥1\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}}\geq 1 and Λgap≥1\Lambda_{\mathrm{gap}}\geq 1 such that, for every non-root node vv and every K≥0K\geq 0,

∑j=0KΓv(j)​(δv)≤Λpre​Γv(K)​(δv),\sum_{j=0}^{K}\Gamma_{v}^{(j)}(\delta_{v})\leq\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}}\Gamma_{v}^{(K)}(\delta_{v}), (10)

and, for every non-root node vv,

Γv​(Δveff2,δv)≤Λgap​Γv​(Δveff,δv).\Gamma_{v}\!\left(\frac{\Delta_{v}^{\mathrm{eff}}}{2},\delta_{v}\right)\leq\Lambda_{\mathrm{gap}}\,\Gamma_{v}(\Delta_{v}^{\mathrm{eff}},\delta_{v}). (11)

We write Λloc≔Λpre​Λgap\Lambda_{\mathrm{loc}}\coloneqq\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}}\Lambda_{\mathrm{gap}}.

Remark 3.4.

Assumption 3.3 is purely local: it does not compare the raw recursive dyadic DP with J∗J^{*}. The prefix condition is the standard dyadic regularity of a statistical sample-complexity curve; it holds with a constant for polynomial laws, e.g., mv​(ρ,δv)≍ρ−2​log⁡(1/δv)m_{v}(\rho,\delta_{v})\asymp\rho^{-2}\log(1/\delta_{v}) with uniform comparison constants over the positive-cost scales. The second condition only asks that moving from the effective gap to the neighboring dyadic half-scale changes the local stop cost by at most a constant factor. This is the only place where the deterministic fast-bias cutoff in Eq. (7) can create a knife-edge, which is ruled out by the assumption at the exact effective gap.

Lemma 3.5.

For a fixed nondecreasing depth-budget sequence (αh)h=0D(\alpha_{h})_{h=0}^{D} with αh≥1\alpha_{h}\geq 1, define P0=ΛlocP_{0}=\Lambda_{\mathrm{loc}} and, for h≥1h\geq 1,

Ph≔max⁡{(1+αh)​Λloc,(1+Λpreαh)​Ph−1}.P_{h}\coloneqq\max\!\left\{(1+\alpha_{h})\Lambda_{\mathrm{loc}},\,\left(1+\frac{\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}}}{\alpha_{h}}\right)P_{h-1}\right\}. (12)

With the concrete choice αh=(h+1)2\alpha_{h}=(h+1)^{2}, this recursion gives PD=𝒪Λpre,Λgap​(D2)P_{D}=\mathcal{O}_{\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}},\Lambda_{\mathrm{gap}}}(D^{2}).

Proof. We denote A=ΛlocA=\Lambda_{\mathrm{loc}} and B=ΛpreB=\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}}, and unrolling the recursion shows that PDP_{D} is at most the largest local term (1+αi)​A(1+\alpha_{i})A, multiplied by the product of later recursive multipliers:

PD≤A​max0≤i≤D​[(1+αi)​∏j=i+1D(1+Bαj)].P_{D}\leq A\max_{0\leq i\leq D}\left[\bigl(1+\alpha_{i}\bigr)\prod_{j=i+1}^{D}\left(1+\frac{B}{\alpha_{j}}\right)\right].

For αj=(j+1)2\alpha_{j}=(j+1)^{2}, the product is bounded by

∏j=1D(1+B(j+1)2)≤exp⁡(B​∑j=1∞1(j+1)2),\prod_{j=1}^{D}\left(1+\frac{B}{(j+1)^{2}}\right)\leq\exp\!\left(B\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(j+1)^{2}}\right),

which is a constant depending only on BB. Since maxi≤D⁡(1+αi)=O⁡(D2)\max_{i\leq D}(1+\alpha_{i})=O(D^{2}), we obtain PD=OΛpre,Λgap​(D2)P_{D}=O_{\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}},\Lambda_{\mathrm{gap}}}(D^{2}), which is the key ingredient for the following general-depth cost bound. □\Box

Theorem 3.6 (General-depth upper bound).

Fix any feasible confidence allocation 𝛅=(δv)v∈𝒯∖{r}\boldsymbol{\delta}=(\delta_{v})_{v\in\mathcal{T}\setminus\{r\}} satisfying Assumption 3.3, and run Algorithm 1 with ε=0\varepsilon=0. On ℰδ\mathcal{E}_{\delta}, the algorithm is guaranteed to stop at a finite time τ\tau, returns a^τ=a∗\hat{a}_{\tau}=a^{*}, and satisfies Cτ≤PD​H​(𝛅)C_{\tau}\leq P_{D}\,H(\boldsymbol{\delta}).

With the depth budgets αh=(h+1)2\alpha_{h}=(h+1)^{2}, the cost Cτ≤𝒪Λpre,Λgap​(D2​H​(𝛅))C_{\tau}\leq\mathcal{O}_{\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}},\Lambda_{\mathrm{gap}}}\!\left(D^{2}H(\boldsymbol{\delta})\right). Consequently, suppose the regularity constants Λpre\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}} and Λgap\Lambda_{\mathrm{gap}} are uniform along a near-optimal feasible sequence: for every η>0\eta>0, there exists a feasible allocation 𝛅η\boldsymbol{\delta}^{\eta} satisfying Assumption 3.3 with these same constants and

H⁡(𝜹η)≤H∗+η.H(\boldsymbol{\delta}^{\eta})\leq H^{*}+\eta.

Then, the corresponding run satisfies, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

a^τ=a∗,Cτ≤PD​(H∗+η).\hat{a}_{\tau}=a^{*},\qquad C_{\tau}\leq P_{D}\bigl(H^{*}+\eta\bigr).

In particular, when αh=(h+1)2\alpha_{h}=(h+1)^{2} and the local regularity constants are uniform constants,

Cτ≤𝒪Λpre,Λgap​(D2​(H∗+η)),C_{\tau}\leq\mathcal{O}_{\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}},\Lambda_{\mathrm{gap}}}\!\left(D^{2}(H^{*}+\eta)\right),

and, since H∗≥|Ch⁡(r)|≥2H^{*}\geq|\mathrm{Ch}(r)|\geq 2, one obtains 𝒪Λpre,Λgap​(D2​H∗)\mathcal{O}_{\Lambda_{\mathrm{pre}},\Lambda_{\mathrm{gap}}}(D^{2}H^{*}) by taking η≤H∗\eta\leq H^{*}, or η=0\eta=0 whenever the infimum in Eq. (9) is attained with the same regularity constants.

Proof sketch. To our knowledge, this is the first theoretical result to establish a bound for multi-fidelity bandit in the tree setting. We therefore hope the proof structure sets up a paradigm for future work, and Theorem 3.6 is proved formally in Appendix B.6. Overall, we have one main goal: charge the actual oracle calls made by 2FFS to the ideal recursive oracle complexity H⁡(𝜹)H(\boldsymbol{\delta}). First, every certificate used by 2FFS is shown to be sound: once a side of a node is certified at scale kk, the corresponding endpoint error is at most ρk/2\rho_{k}/2. Second, a recursive call is shown to spend effort only on children that can still affect the parent certificate at the current scale; since child calls are capped by the parent scale, the algorithm avoids irrelevant fine-scale work below already separated parts of the tree. Third, for each node and scale, the budgeted resolver spends at most a local certification budget plus its recursive budget, and the same node-side-scale is never charged again after certification. Summing these charges over active scales, while reserving the cap needed for the next step, gives a subtree bound with overhead Ph⁡(v)P_{h(v)}. Lemma 3.5 then shows that this overhead is only quadratic in depth for αh=(h+1)2\alpha_{h}=(h+1)^{2}. Applying the subtree bound to the root children gives a finite global cost bound; since every non-stopping round makes positive progress, the algorithm must stop, and interval validity gives correctness.

3.2 Guarantees for real-world multi-agent RL application

In many real-world applications, e.g., multi-agent RL (MARL) with minimax trees, slow oracles may not provide perfectly unbiased estimates of the minimax value V∗V^{*}, and a tight, accurate fast-oracle envelope BB may be unavailable and must instead be approximated by a proxy. In this section, we establish additional theoretical guarantees for such imperfect real-world settings.

Biased slow oracles.

We show that pointwise slow-oracle bias can be handled without accumulation across tree depths. Specifically, Theorem 3.7 gives a correctness guarantee using a known bias bound.

Theorem 3.7.

Suppose the slow oracle has fixed mean V∗​(v)+bvV^{*}(v)+b_{v}, with known ξ≥maxv⁡|bv|\xi\geq\max_{v}|b_{v}|, and its samples satisfy Eq. (3) around this mean. Replacing each slow radius βv\beta_{v} by βv+ξ\beta_{v}+\xi preserves the (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta) finite-output correctness of 2FFS. The bias inflation does not accumulate with tree depth.

Loose fast-oracle envelope.

In practical MARL applications, the true minimax value is unavailable, and thus a tight fast-oracle envelope cannot be constructed. Instead, one can use a calibrated proxy envelope that shrinks with the remaining horizon, for example,

B^​(h)=1+h−1D−1,B^​(0)=0,\hat{B}(h)=1+\frac{h-1}{D-1},\qquad\hat{B}(0)=0,

where D≥2D\geq 2 is the full tree depth and h≥1h\geq 1 is the remaining depth, provided B^​(h)≥B​(h)\hat{B}(h)\geq B(h). We show that such a loose envelope preserves the PAC guarantee.

Theorem 3.8.

Let B⁡(h)B(h) denote the true fast-oracle envelope, and let B^​(h)\hat{B}(h) be a nondecreasing proxy envelope with B^​(0)=0\hat{B}(0)=0 and B^​(h)≥B​(h)\hat{B}(h)\geq B(h) for all hh. Replacing B⁡(h)B(h) with B^​(h)\hat{B}(h) preserves the finite-output PAC guarantee and, on ℰδ\mathcal{E}_{\delta} for the same query history, can only widen the resulting confidence intervals.

The proofs and qualifications for both results are given in Appendix B.7.

4 Numerical Experiments

We evaluate 2FFS on stochastic minimax trees, focusing on whether it can reduce search effort by adaptively combining cheap biased evaluations with expensive accurate samples. We compare against three fixed-confidence baselines: (i) BAI-MCTS sampling (BAI-MCTS) [5], which uses stochastic leaf samples; (ii) minimax fast-oracle (Minimax-fast), which uses only the deterministic fast oracle; and (iii) fixed-depth expansion followed by slow-oracle sampling on the exposed frontier (Slow-only). The second and third baselines are controlled ablations: they test, respectively, the limits of relying only on fast expansion and of committing to a non-adaptive expansion depth before slow sampling. We use the abbreviated names in parentheses in all tables. We note that BAI-MCTS [5, §4] has shown that it already substantially improves (15×\times) over earlier tree-based BAI methods, including UGapE-MCTS [19], LUCB-MCTS [20], and FindTopWinner [21].

Setup and evaluation.

Our main experiments use balanced bb-ary minimax trees with (D,b)∈{(5,8),(7,6),(10,3)}(D,b)\in\{(5,8),(7,6),(10,3)\}, with 100100 independently generated trees per setting. These configurations cover both wide shallow trees and deeper narrower trees, and are much larger than the depth-33, 1010-ary setting (only 11111111 nodes) in BAI-MCTS [5], with more explicit evidence of efficiency improvement.

For evaluation, we report two complementary metrics. The first is sampling count, the total number of nodes sampled and visited. The second is operation count, the total number of bookkeeping operation units, where one operation count is one 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) scalar state access, update, or comparison. This distinction is important because sampling one node does not necessarily induce the same amount of computation across methods. For example, after a stochastic leaf sample, BAI-MCTS mainly updates the sampled leaf interval and propagates confidence bounds along the leaf-to-root path. In contrast, after a slow oracle sample, 2FFS updates local slow intervals, intersects them with fast intervals, propagates minimax bounds, and maintains scale-dependent comparison certificates. Thus, sampling count measures efficiency of repetitive nodes visit, while operation count measures the overall computation efficiency.

Results.

Table 1 shows that 2FFS substantially reduces search effort relative to the BAI-MCTS baseline: across the reported settings, it uses 160160–1450×1450\times fewer sampled or visited nodes and 1.91.9–4.6×4.6\times fewer bookkeeping operations. The ablations illustrate the two sides of the fast–slow tradeoff. Minimax-fast is computationally cheap because it relies only on fast expansion, but this efficiency comes at the cost of accuracy since the fast oracle is biased. Conversely, Slow-only uses accurate slow-oracle samples and can be accurate when enough samples are collected, but it requires many more samples and often fails to stop within the finite budget. Overall, these results suggest that 2FFS gains its efficiency by adaptively choosing when to trust fast expansion and when to spend slow samples on decision-critical nodes.

Ablations.

We further test the sensitivity of 2FFS to the fast-oracle bias and slow-oracle noise. Using D=5D=5, 8-ary trees, we sweep the fast-oracle bias with mean 0.450.45 and the slow-oracle noise with mean 0.010.01. Figure 2 shows that 2FFS is relatively stable across both ranges, suggesting that its performance is not overly sensitive to moderate changes in either oracle parameter.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we introduced 2FFS, a two-fidelity algorithm for fixed-confidence best-action identification in stochastic minimax trees. Our work bridges multi-fidelity bandits and minimax tree search by providing a principled mechanism for adaptively trading off cheap biased expansion against expensive accurate sampling. Theoretically, we prove PAC correctness, finite stopping, and a general-depth cost bound relative to an ideal recursive oracle complexity. Empirically, 2FFS achieves substantial gains in sampling efficiency over BAI-MCTS-style baselines while maintaining reliable root-action identification. These results suggest that two-fidelity tree search may be a useful abstraction beyond the current theoretical framework, with potential applications in multi-agent reinforcement learning, game-tree planning, and LLM policy-rollout systems, where accurate rollouts are expensive but cheap heuristic evaluations are widely available, a further discussion to these is provided in Appendix A.

Follow-up work.

We note that 2FFS opens up a broad range of potential directions for future work. On the empirical side, we suggest investigating how 2FFS can be integrated with policy-gradient-based MARL, particularly how to design approximate envelopes that ensure the effectiveness of fast oracles. Such extensions could also be explored for training LLMs in multi-agent environments, such as chess playing and adversarial training. On the theoretical side, we first look forward to seeing how 2FFS can be adapted to non-minimax trees, which could facilitate extensions to tree-of-thought rollout structures for expansive LLM reasoning trajectories. Beyond this direction, within minimax trees, we also look forward to further developments in fast-oracle envelope design, as well as weaker assumptions for the cost upper bound, or even tighter upper bounds.

Appendix A Further Related Works and Limitations

Multi-fidelity bandits and optimization.

Multi-fidelity methods study how to allocate queries across information sources with different costs and accuracies. In flat bandit models, the goal is typically to identify or compete with the best arm while using cheap biased fidelities when they are informative and reserving expensive accurate fidelities for difficult comparisons [1, 2, 3, 4]. Related ideas also appear in multi-fidelity Bayesian and black-box optimization, where low-cost simulators, subsampled training runs, or surrogate evaluations are used to accelerate optimization under a total cost budget [11, 12, 22, 23, 24, 25]. These works provide the broad cost–accuracy motivation for our two-oracle model, but they do not address minimax value propagation through an adversarial tree or fixed-confidence certification of a root action.

Relation to multi-fidelity tree search for noisy black-box optimization.

Sen et al. [26] study noisy black-box optimization with multi-fidelity queries using a tree-search approach. Their tree is a hierarchical partition of the input domain of an unknown function; a node represents a region of the search space, and querying at a fidelity gives a biased and noisy estimate useful for optimistic optimization. Their algorithms, MFHOO and MFPOO, adapt HOO/POO-style optimistic tree search to continuous fidelities and are analyzed through simple regret under a finite cost budget.

This is related in spirit because both settings combine tree search with multi-fidelity information, but it is not the same problem. In our setting, the tree is not an auxiliary partition of a black-box domain: it is the stochastic minimax tree itself, with alternating Max/Min backups and a root-action decision. Our objective is fixed-confidence (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-PAC best-action identification, not simple-regret minimization after a budget is exhausted. Methodologically, 2FFS maintains valid confidence intervals at minimax nodes, propagates them through adversarial backups, and adaptively chooses between local slow certification and recursive fast expansion. This differs from the optimistic partition-refinement mechanism of MFHOO/MFPOO, where the tree is used to explore a continuous domain and there is no minimax alternation, no root-child certification problem, and no two-route local-versus-recursive certificate of the kind used here.

Best-action identification and tree-based planning.

Pure-exploration bandits distinguish fixed-budget regret-style objectives from fixed-confidence identification objectives. The flat best-arm identification literature characterizes instance-dependent sample complexity for identifying the best arm [18, 27], with extensions to structured settings such as unimodal bandits [28, 29] and cost-aware sampling [30]. In tree-based planning, classical minimax search and α\alpha-β\beta pruning exploit deterministic backups in adversarial trees [6, 7], while MCTS uses stochastic sampling and bandit-style selection rules [8]. BAI-MCTS [5] brings fixed-confidence identification to minimax trees, but assumes a single unbiased sampling oracle. Our contribution combines this fixed-confidence root-action perspective with a calibrated cheap evaluator and an expensive accurate evaluator.

Applications and oracle-based learning.

Multi-fidelity ideas are widely used in hyperparameter optimization [31, 32, 33, 34], medical trial design [35], and engineering design problems such as hydrofoil, wind-farm, and aerodynamic optimization [36, 37, 38]. More broadly, oracle-based learning studies how decision-making systems can exploit structured feedback such as ranking or comparison oracles [39, 40]. Our work fits this broader line by studying how cheap heuristic information and expensive reliable feedback should be allocated in a structured decision tree and GDA-style minimax tree [41].

Future work.

We acknowledge several limitations, which also open a broad space for follow-up work from both empirical and theoretical perspectives. Empirically, our experiments focus on simulated finite minimax trees, while many modern planning problems involve richer interactive environments (we note that adapting 2FFS to these areas would require the effort of a fully new follow-up work). Extending 2FFS to multi-agent reinforcement learning, policy-gradient-based training, or neural-guided MCTS would be an important step toward broader applications, but is beyond the scope of the present paper. In addition, our current formulation assumes finite trees with fixed depth (which aligns with the setup from previous tree-based BAI works); adapting the method to dynamically generated trees, progressive widening, or very large action spaces is a natural next direction. We also note such minimax planning can be smoothly integrated with the recent group-based language model policy optimization for language model reasoning [42, 43, 44, 45] and language model alignment and decision making problems [46, 47].

Theoretically, our general-depth upper bound relies on mild local regularity assumptions on the sampling complexity. Understanding whether these conditions can be weakened, verified adaptively, or replaced by fully data-dependent stopping criteria would further sharpen the theory. Another important direction is to close the remaining gap between the current polynomial-depth factor and the ideal recursive oracle complexity, potentially leading to tighter depth dependence or sharper instance-dependent bounds.

B.3 Full 2FFS Details

We now give the full version of Algorithm 1. The resolver Resolve​(v,s,k,B)\textsc{Resolve}(v,s,k,B) includes an invocation-level cost cap BB, omitted from the main-text pseudocode. This cap prevents a child call from exceeding the remaining budget inherited from its parent. All ties use fixed deterministic node and side orders, independent of the invocation cap and of ε\varepsilon.

To define the algorithm on every sample path, fix a default root action in advance. If an interval intersection becomes empty, terminate the entire run immediately and return this default action, before evaluating any widths or certificates. This exceptional rule never applies on ℰδ\mathcal{E}_{\delta} by Lemma 2.4; any error caused by it is therefore included in the confidence-failure event. All subsequent interval and scale operations are performed only while the intervals are nonempty.

The algorithm allows local reversibility: once a node vv has been exposed, it may receive direct slow samples at vv even after expansion. Thus the two certification routes at vv,

  • •

    the local route, which shrinks Ivloc​(t)I_{v}^{\mathrm{loc}}(t) through slow samples at vv, and

  • •

    the recursive route, which shrinks Ivch​(t)I_{v}^{\mathrm{ch}}(t) by expanding below vv and recursively refining its children,

remain available throughout the run. Work performed below vv and samples taken at vv both contribute to its effective interval.

The algorithm uses the dyadic target diameters (ρk)k≥0(\rho_{k})_{k\geq 0} from §2: scale kk means target width ρk/2\rho_{k}/2, and Γv(k)​(δv)=Γv​(ρk,δv)\Gamma_{v}^{(k)}(\delta_{v})=\Gamma_{v}(\rho_{k},\delta_{v}) is the corresponding local stopping cost.

Each outer-loop iteration computes an active local scale for the current leader and challenger, then selects a root-side obligation as specified below. A node vv is resolved at scale kk once the targeted side has an observable certificate at tolerance ρk/2\rho_{k}/2.

The choice between local sampling and recursion is governed by a budget. Fix a nondecreasing polynomial depth-budget sequence

αh≥1,h=0,1,…,D,\alpha_{h}\geq 1,\qquad h=0,1,\ldots,D,

for example αh=(h+1)2\alpha_{h}=(h+1)^{2}. For an internal node vv, the recursive route at scale kk is allowed to spend at most

𝖡v,krec≔αh⁡(v)​Γv(k)​(δv)\mathsf{B}_{v,k}^{\mathrm{rec}}\coloneqq\alpha_{h(v)}\,\Gamma_{v}^{(k)}(\delta_{v})

below vv, before the obligation falls back to direct slow sampling at vv. The resolver first attempts recursive work and falls back to local sampling when its recursive budget is insufficient. To track spending at each explored non-root node vv and scale kk, define

Mv,kloc​(t)≔c×(number of slow queries issued at v while resolving scale k),M_{v,k}^{\mathrm{loc}}(t)\coloneqq c\times\bigl(\text{number of slow queries issued at $v$ while resolving scale $k$}\bigr),

and Mv,kexp​(t)M_{v,k}^{\mathrm{exp}}(t) as the total cost already spent strictly below vv while resolving the scale-kk recursive obligation at vv.

These counters record costs already incurred. The recursive counter enforces the budget, while the current certificates determine which child to refine. Together, these rules limit spending below a node and direct it toward children that still affect the required comparison.

At the root, let

at∈argmaxa∈Ch⁡(r)La​(t),bt∈argmaxa∈Ch⁡(r)∖{at}Ua​(t)a_{t}\in\mathop{\rm argmax}_{a\in\mathrm{Ch}(r)}L_{a}(t),\qquad b_{t}\in\mathop{\rm argmax}_{a\in\mathrm{Ch}(r)\setminus\{a_{t}\}}U_{a}(t)

be the current leader and challenger. 2FFS stops once some root action beats every competitor up to ε\varepsilon, i.e.,

stop if there exists ​a^t∈Ch⁡(r)​ such that ​La^t​(t)≥maxa≠a^t⁡Ua​(t)−ε.\text{stop if there exists }\hat{a}_{t}\in\mathrm{Ch}(r)\text{ such that }L_{\hat{a}_{t}}(t)\geq\max_{a\neq\hat{a}_{t}}U_{a}(t)-\varepsilon.

Otherwise, 2FFS refines one uncertified decision-critical root side.

The challenger may either be excluded or become the leader. The algorithm therefore computes the current lower-side scale for the leader ata_{t} and the current full-contender scale for the challenger btb_{t}, then selects the obligation with the coarser unresolved diameter.

Inside the selected subtree, the algorithm first attempts recursive work. If the node’s own recursive budget prevents progress, the resolver falls back to a direct slow sample, provided its inherited cap permits that sample. If the inherited cap prevents the chosen action, the call returns without spending. In the two selector cases (Min,L)(\textsc{Min},L) and (Max,U)(\textsc{Max},U), the recursive route selects an unresolved endpoint witness. In the two comparison cases (Max,L)(\textsc{Max},L) and (Min,U)(\textsc{Min},U), it selects the child whose endpoint most strongly obstructs the parent-side comparison certificate.

An internal blocker is refined through obligations capped at the parent scale. A call may improve either the parent’s comparison side or the opposite endpoint used to exclude the blocker. It cannot use a finer scale than the parent obligation. This restriction is what allows the localization bound below to remain independent of depth.

For an expanded internal node vv, define the scale-aware active child set As​(v,k,t)⊆Ch⁡(v)A_{s}(v,k,t)\subseteq\mathrm{Ch}(v) as follows. In the two selector cases, we use the endpoint witness sets:

  • •

    if s=Ls=L and vv is a Min node, then

    AL​(v,k,t)=argminu∈Ch⁡(v)Lu​(t);A_{L}(v,k,t)=\mathop{\rm argmin}_{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}L_{u}(t);
  • •

    if s=Us=U and vv is a Max node, then

    AU​(v,k,t)=argmaxu∈Ch⁡(v)Uu​(t);A_{U}(v,k,t)=\mathop{\rm argmax}_{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}U_{u}(t);

In the two comparison cases we instead compare against the current best comparison endpoint and define a lazy set of critical children:

  • •

    if s=Ls=L and vv is a Max node, let

    AL(v,k,t)={u∈Ch(v):Uu(t)>λL(v,t)+ρk/2and¬𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉L(u,k,t)};A_{L}(v,k,t)=\bigl\{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v):\,U_{u}(t)>\lambda_{L}(v,t)+\rho_{k}/2\ \text{and}\ \neg\mathsf{Comp}_{L}(u,k,t)\bigr\};
  • •

Therefore, As​(v,k,t)A_{s}(v,k,t) contains only the children that are still unresolved at the current scale for the comparison required by the parent. In a comparison case, a child is discharged either by endpoint exclusion, namely falling outside the displayed margin, or by same-side completion at scale kk. A discharged child is no longer recursively refined for that parent-scale obligation. Equivalently, the two comparison certificates use the following dual discharge rules:

When (v,s)(v,s) is a comparison case and As​(v,k,t)≠∅A_{s}(v,k,t)\neq\varnothing, define the current blocking contender by

{bL​(v,k,t)∈argmaxu∈AL​(v,k,t)Uu​(t),if ​v​ is a Max node and ​s=L,bU​(v,k,t)∈argminu∈AU​(v,k,t)Lu​(t),if ​v​ is a Min node and ​s=U.\begin{cases}b_{L}(v,k,t)\in\mathop{\rm argmax}_{u\in A_{L}(v,k,t)}U_{u}(t),&\text{if }v\text{ is a {Max} node and }s=L,\\[4.0pt] b_{U}(v,k,t)\in\mathop{\rm argmin}_{u\in A_{U}(v,k,t)}L_{u}(t),&\text{if }v\text{ is a {Min} node and }s=U.\end{cases}

2FFS maintains scale-local side-completion flags 𝖣𝗈𝗇𝖾s​(v,k)∈{0,1}\mathsf{Done}_{s}(v,k)\in\{0,1\}. These flags are initialized to 00 when the pair (v,k)(v,k) is first used, and are only changed from 00 to 11. When used as a predicate, 𝖣𝗈𝗇𝖾s​(v,k,t)\mathsf{Done}_{s}(v,k,t) denotes that the flag is equal to 11 at round tt. An unstored flag is interpreted as zero; storage is initialized before any assignment to it.

In a comparison case, the children in As​(v,k,t)A_{s}(v,k,t) are exactly those that are neither endpoint-excluded nor same-side complete at scale kk.

Among them, only the current blocker bs​(v,k,t)b_{s}(v,k,t) is eligible for recursive comparison work. The blocker may be refined either on the parent-targeted side ss, which supports promotion or same-side safety, or on the opposite side s¯\bar{s}, which supports endpoint exclusion, but both calls are capped by the current parent scale kk. Note that no child is required to become fully complete merely because it is currently active.

width⁡(Ivloc​(t))≤ρk/2,\mathrm{width}\bigl(I_{v}^{\mathrm{loc}}(t)\bigr)\leq\rho_{k}/2,

For leaves, only the first two alternatives can apply. Finally, the following are equivalent

Otherwise, the search has a finite upper limit. To see this, collect the strictly positive values among all current effective and local interval widths and all comparison differences Uu−λL​(v,t)U_{u}-\lambda_{L}(v,t) and λU​(v,t)−Lu\lambda_{U}(v,t)-L_{u} appearing in the certificate formulas. The root selection is also well-defined outside ℰδ\mathcal{E}_{\delta} while all intervals remain nonempty. Indeed, bottom-up induction gives

ZL​(v,t)​and​ZU​(v,t)⟹Uv​(t)=Lv​(t).Z_{L}(v,t)\ \text{and}\ Z_{U}(v,t)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad U_{v}(t)=L_{v}(t).

If either zero-tolerance predicate uses a width alternative, this is immediate. Otherwise, suppose both predicates hold recursively but vv has positive width. By induction Uu=Lu≤maxx⁡LxU_{u}=L_{u}\leq\max_{x}L_{x}, a contradiction. The Min case is dual, using a child in argminxLx\mathop{\rm argmin}_{x}L_{x}. An unexpanded node has no recursive certificate, which supplies the induction base. The finite search above therefore shows that a positive-width node cannot have both KL=KU=+∞K_{L}=K_{U}=+\infty. Thus the selected root obligation is finite on every path on which the algorithm has not already terminated.

For a finite parent scale kk, define the capped unresolved scale

Ks≤k​(x,t)≔min⁡{0≤j≤k:¬𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉s​(x,j,t)},K_{s}^{\leq k}(x,t)\coloneqq\min\{0\leq j\leq k:\ \neg\mathsf{Comp}_{s}(x,j,t)\},

A recursive call made while resolving a parent obligation at scale kk may only call a child at a capped scale Ks′≤k​(u,t)K_{s^{\prime}}^{\leq k}(u,t).

Thus, recursive descent can refine a child at a coarser unresolved scale, but never at a scale finer than the current parent obligation.

The root challenger has no parent scale to cap its obligations. Its contender side is defined as follows. If at least one of KL​(u,t)K_{L}(u,t) and KU​(u,t)K_{U}(u,t) is finite, set

breaking ties arbitrarily, and define its contender scale by

K±​(u,t)≔Kσ⁡(u,t)​(u,t).K_{\pm}(u,t)\coloneqq K_{\sigma(u,t)}(u,t).

If both KL​(u,t)K_{L}(u,t) and KU​(u,t)K_{U}(u,t) are +∞+\infty, we set σ⁡(u,t)=U\sigma(u,t)=U arbitrarily and K±​(u,t)=+∞K_{\pm}(u,t)=+\infty. In this case, the contender has no unresolved root-side obligation.

A full-contender call then uses Resolve​(u,σ⁡(u,t),K±​(u,t)).\textsc{Resolve}(u,\sigma(u,t),K_{\pm}(u,t)). For internal comparison blockers, we instead use capped side obligations. Write L¯=U\bar{L}=U and U¯=L\bar{U}=L. During Resolve​(v,s,k)\textsc{Resolve}(v,s,k), an internal blocker bs​(v,k,t)b_{s}(v,k,t) is first called on the opposite side s¯\bar{s} at scale Ks¯≤k​(bs​(v,k,t),t)K_{\bar{s}}^{\leq k}(b_{s}(v,k,t),t), whenever that capped obligation is finite. This is the endpoint that appears in the exclusion inequality. Only after the blocker has no unresolved opposite-side obligation at scales ≤k\leq k, while remaining active, is it called on the same side ss at scale Ks≤k​(bs​(v,k,t),t)K_{s}^{\leq k}(b_{s}(v,k,t),t).

The same-side blocker obligation can then discharge the blocker through 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉s​(bs,k,t)\mathsf{Comp}_{s}(b_{s},k,t) or allow it to promote through the comparison-side endpoint. When evaluating a finite scale in KsK_{s} or Ks≤kK_{s}^{\leq k}, the EvaluateScale convention above initializes and latches the required scale-local flags. The fourth argument of Resolve​(v,s,k,B)\textsc{Resolve}(v,s,k,B) is an invocation-level cost cap: the call may not perform a positive oracle action whose returned cost would exceed BB. We write Resolve​(v,s,k)\textsc{Resolve}(v,s,k) in the analysis when the cap is irrelevant. Each actual recursive call receives the minimum of the parent obligation’s remaining recursive budget and its inherited invocation cap.

Remark B.1 (Scale-synchronous progress).

Recursive descent is required to remain synchronized with the current parent obligation and its remaining recursive budget. Concretely, inside a call Resolve​(v,s,k,B)\textsc{Resolve}(v,s,k,B), a child call Resolve​(u,s′,Ks′≤k​(u,t),Brec)\textsc{Resolve}(u,s^{\prime},K_{s^{\prime}}^{\leq k}(u,t),B_{\mathrm{rec}}) is admissible only if the scale-kk certificate at vv is still unresolved at the current round, the child is selected by the current scale-kk rule at vv, and BrecB_{\mathrm{rec}} is no larger than the remaining budget 𝖡v,krec−Mv,kexp\mathsf{B}_{v,k}^{\mathrm{rec}}-M_{v,k}^{\mathrm{exp}}. In particular,

  • •

    in a comparison case, the algorithm may refine only the current blocking contender bs​(v,k,t)∈As​(v,k,t)b_{s}(v,k,t)\in A_{s}(v,k,t); the blocker is refined first on (bs​(v,k,t),s¯,Ks¯≤k​(bs​(v,k,t),t))(b_{s}(v,k,t),\bar{s},K_{\bar{s}}^{\leq k}(b_{s}(v,k,t),t)) whenever this obligation is finite, and otherwise on (bs​(v,k,t),s,Ks≤k​(bs​(v,k,t),t))(b_{s}(v,k,t),s,K_{s}^{\leq k}(b_{s}(v,k,t),t));

  • •

    in a selector case, the algorithm may refine only a child u∈As​(v,k,t)u\in A_{s}(v,k,t) with ¬𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉s​(u,k,t)\neg\mathsf{Comp}_{s}(u,k,t), and it calls that child at Ks≤k​(u,t)K_{s}^{\leq k}(u,t).

Every invocation of Resolve​(v,s,k,B)\textsc{Resolve}(v,s,k,B) performs at most one positive oracle action, either a slow query or an expansion, at the current node or below it. A local query may follow a zero-cost blocked child return. After each positive action, the algorithm updates the intervals, comparison endpoints, blockers, and active child sets before descending again. Thus the coarser-scale tests that could already certify or exclude a child from the current scale-kk obligation are checked before that child is refined further.

The implementation below is split into reusable routines. Algorithm 2 contains scale and selection utilities, Algorithm 3 contains the atomic oracle actions, Algorithm 4 is the budgeted recursive resolver, and Algorithm 5 is the short top-level driver.

Lazy critical children.

In the selector cases, the live sets reduce to the current endpoint witness set. In the comparison cases, a child is discharged once it is endpoint-excluded by the scale-kk comparison margin or same-side complete at scale kk. Among the still-live children, only the endpoint-most blocker is eligible for recursive comparison work. This blocker is refined through capped side obligations only, so it may either become safe on the comparison side or be excluded through the opposite endpoint without being pushed to a finer scale than the parent.

B.4 Proof of Theorem 3.1

Proof. By Eq. (5) and the union bound in §2,

ℙ⁡(ℰδ)≥1−δ.\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{\delta})\geq 1-\delta.

We prove that no ε\varepsilon-incorrect finite recommendation can occur on ℰδ\mathcal{E}_{\delta}. Fix an outcome in ℰδ\mathcal{E}_{\delta} and suppose the algorithm stops at a finite time τ\tau. Let a^τ\hat{a}_{\tau} be any returned root child. Interval validity rules out the exceptional empty-intersection exit on this outcome. Hence the ordinary stopping rule gives

La^τ​(τ)≥maxa≠a^τ⁡Ua​(τ)−ε.L_{\hat{a}_{\tau}}(\tau)\geq\max_{a\neq\hat{a}_{\tau}}U_{a}(\tau)-\varepsilon.

Interval validity holds simultaneously at every round, so Lemma 2.4 also applies at the finite stopping time τ\tau. For every a∈Ch⁡(r)a\in\mathrm{Ch}(r),

La​(τ)≤V∗​(r,a)≤Ua​(τ).L_{a}(\tau)\leq V^{*}(r,a)\leq U_{a}(\tau).

Combining validity with the stopping inequality gives

V∗​(r,a^τ)≥La^τ​(τ)≥maxa≠a^τ⁡Ua​(τ)−ε≥maxa≠a^τ⁡V∗​(r,a)−ε.V^{*}(r,\hat{a}_{\tau})\geq L_{\hat{a}_{\tau}}(\tau)\geq\max_{a\neq\hat{a}_{\tau}}U_{a}(\tau)-\varepsilon\geq\max_{a\neq\hat{a}_{\tau}}V^{*}(r,a)-\varepsilon.

If a^τ=a∗\hat{a}_{\tau}=a^{*}, then the returned action is optimal. Otherwise a∗≠a^τa^{*}\neq\hat{a}_{\tau}, and the last display with a=a∗a=a^{*} gives

V∗​(r,a∗)−V∗​(r,a^τ)≤ε.V^{*}(r,a^{*})-V^{*}(r,\hat{a}_{\tau})\leq\varepsilon.

Thus, every finite recommendation on ℰδ\mathcal{E}_{\delta} is ε\varepsilon-optimal, and the error event in the theorem is contained in ℰδc\mathcal{E}_{\delta}^{c}, whose probability is at most δ\delta. □\Box

B.5 Derived Lemmas for the General-Depth Bound

We first establish soundness of the side certificates and then show that recursive calls remain at scales compatible with the effective gaps. These facts will support the cost bound in Theorem 3.6. Throughout, we work on the simultaneous-validity event ℰδ\mathcal{E}_{\delta}, set ε=0\varepsilon=0, and use Assumption 3.3 only in the aggregate summation and charging steps. All dyadic statements below concern ρ0>0\rho_{0}>0. If ρ0=0\rho_{0}=0, then B⁡(D−1)=0B(D-1)=0 and monotonicity of BB gives B⁡(h⁡(v))=0B(h(v))=0 for every non-root node. Initialization already identifies the optimal root action, and every Γv​(Δveff,δv)\Gamma_{v}(\Delta_{v}^{\mathrm{eff}},\delta_{v}) and Jv∗J_{v}^{*} is zero. Hence Cτ=H⁡(𝜹)=|Ch⁡(r)|C_{\tau}=H(\boldsymbol{\delta})=|\mathrm{Ch}(r)|, without evaluating any dyadic cost at zero precision or requiring dyadic regularity.

The certificates control one endpoint at a time. We use the following notion of safety to express that control.

Definition B.1 (Side-specific scale safety).

Fix a scale index k≥0k\geq 0, a round tt, an explored non-root node vv, and a side s∈{L,U}s\in\{L,U\}. We say that vv is (s,k)(s,k)-safe at round tt if

{V∗​(v)−Lv​(t)≤ρk/2,if ​s=L,Uv​(t)−V∗​(v)≤ρk/2,if ​s=U.\begin{cases}V^{*}(v)-L_{v}(t)\leq\rho_{k}/2,&\text{if }s=L,\\[4.0pt] U_{v}(t)-V^{*}(v)\leq\rho_{k}/2,&\text{if }s=U.\end{cases}

On ℰδ\mathcal{E}_{\delta}, both one-sided errors in Definition B.1 are nonnegative by Lemma 2.4. Moreover, if

Uv​(t)−Lv​(t)≤ρk/2,U_{v}(t)-L_{v}(t)\leq\rho_{k}/2,

then vv is both (L,k)(L,k)-safe and (U,k)(U,k)-safe.

Lemma B.2 (Nested interval updates).

For every node vv whose effective interval is defined at round tt including the root, the effective intervals are nested over time: if t′≥tt^{\prime}\geq t, then

Iv​(t′)⊆Iv​(t).I_{v}(t^{\prime})\subseteq I_{v}(t).

Equivalently, Lv​(t′)≥Lv​(t)L_{v}(t^{\prime})\geq L_{v}(t) and Uv​(t′)≤Uv​(t)U_{v}(t^{\prime})\leq U_{v}(t). The same nesting holds for Ivloc​(t)I_{v}^{\mathrm{loc}}(t) whenever v≠rv\neq r is exposed by round tt.

Proof. We check the local intervals first, then propagate nesting up the explored tree. At an exposed non-root node, the fast interval is fixed, while the running intersection in Eq. (4) can only shrink as slow samples arrive. Therefore Ivloc​(t)=IvF∩IvS​(t)I_{v}^{\mathrm{loc}}(t)=I_{v}^{F}\cap I_{v}^{S}(t) is nested.

For the child backups, both minimax operators preserve the required endpoint monotonicity. At a Max node, the lower endpoint maxu⁡Lu​(t)\max_{u}L_{u}(t) is nondecreasing and the upper endpoint maxu⁡Uu​(t)\max_{u}U_{u}(t) is nonincreasing whenever every child interval is nested.

At a Min node, the corresponding endpoints are minu⁡Lu​(t)\min_{u}L_{u}(t) and minu⁡Uu​(t)\min_{u}U_{u}(t), with the same monotonicity. Induction from the leaves of the explored tree therefore shows that Ivch​(t)I_{v}^{\mathrm{ch}}(t) is nested after expansion. Before expansion it is (−∞,+∞)(-\infty,+\infty), so the first expansion preserves nesting as well. Intersecting the local and child-backup intervals proves the claim for Iv​(t)I_{v}(t) at every non-root node. At the root, the effective interval is the child backup itself. □\Box

Interval nesting preserves an endpoint-accuracy guarantee once established. We now verify that the side certificates provide such a guarantee.

Lemma B.3 (Comparison-certificate soundness).

Fix a round tt, a scale index k≥0k\geq 0, an explored non-root node vv, and a side s∈{L,U}s\in\{L,U\}. On ℰδ\mathcal{E}_{\delta}, if 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉s​(v,k,t)\mathsf{Comp}_{s}(v,k,t) holds, then vv is (s,k)(s,k)-safe at round tt.

Proof. We induct on the remaining depth h⁡(v)h(v), with the induction claim uniform over all rounds, scales, and sides: whenever 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉s​(v,k,t)\mathsf{Comp}_{s}(v,k,t) holds, vv is (s,k)(s,k)-safe at round tt. Fix vv and assume the claim for every child of vv. We first verify the current certificate 𝖢𝖾𝗋𝗍s​(v,k,t)\mathsf{Cert}_{s}(v,k,t), then use interval nesting to handle certificates latched at an earlier round.

If

Uv​(t)−Lv​(t)≤ρk/2,U_{v}(t)-L_{v}(t)\leq\rho_{k}/2,

then Lemma 2.4 gives V∗​(v)∈[Lv​(t),Uv​(t)]V^{*}(v)\in[L_{v}(t),U_{v}(t)], so both one-sided errors are at most ρk/2\rho_{k}/2.

If

width⁡(Ivloc​(t))≤ρk/2,\mathrm{width}\bigl(I_{v}^{\mathrm{loc}}(t)\bigr)\leq\rho_{k}/2,

then Iv​(t)⊆Ivloc​(t)I_{v}(t)\subseteq I_{v}^{\mathrm{loc}}(t), while interval validity places V∗​(v)V^{*}(v) in Iv​(t)I_{v}(t). Thus this alternative also bounds both one-sided errors by ρk/2\rho_{k}/2.

It remains to consider 𝖢𝖾𝗋𝗍s​(v,k,t)\mathsf{Cert}_{s}(v,k,t) obtained through the recursive alternative. The selector cases use an endpoint witness; the comparison cases require a bound for every child.

Min node, s=Ls=L. The selector set is

AL​(v,k,t)=arg⁡minu∈Ch⁡(v)​Lu​(t),A_{L}(v,k,t)=\arg\min_{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}L_{u}(t),

which is nonempty. The recursive certificate requires every u∈AL​(v,k,t)u\in A_{L}(v,k,t) to satisfy 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉L​(u,k,t)\mathsf{Comp}_{L}(u,k,t); the induction hypothesis therefore makes each such child (L,k)(L,k)-safe. Choose any x∈AL​(v,k,t)x\in A_{L}(v,k,t). Its endpoint is the selector minimum, and the parent value is no larger than its value:

Lx​(t)=minu∈Ch⁡(v)⁡Lu​(t)andV∗​(v)=minu∈Ch⁡(v)⁡V∗​(u)≤V∗​(x),L_{x}(t)=\min_{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}L_{u}(t)\qquad\text{and}\qquad V^{*}(v)=\min_{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}V^{*}(u)\leq V^{*}(x),

and containment Iv​(t)⊆Ivch​(t)I_{v}(t)\subseteq I_{v}^{\mathrm{ch}}(t) gives

Lv​(t)≥minu∈Ch⁡(v)⁡Lu​(t)=Lx​(t),L_{v}(t)\geq\min_{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}L_{u}(t)=L_{x}(t),

so the selected child’s safety yields

V∗​(v)−Lv​(t)≤V∗​(x)−Lx​(t)≤ρk/2.V^{*}(v)-L_{v}(t)\leq V^{*}(x)-L_{x}(t)\leq\rho_{k}/2.

Max node, s=Us=U. The selector set is

AU​(v,k,t)=arg⁡maxu∈Ch⁡(v)​Uu​(t),A_{U}(v,k,t)=\arg\max_{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}U_{u}(t),

and containment Iv​(t)⊆Ivch​(t)I_{v}(t)\subseteq I_{v}^{\mathrm{ch}}(t) gives

Uv​(t)≤maxu∈Ch⁡(v)⁡Uu​(t)=Ux​(t),U_{v}(t)\leq\max_{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}U_{u}(t)=U_{x}(t),

so the selected child’s safety yields

Uv​(t)−V∗​(v)≤Ux​(t)−V∗​(x)≤ρk/2.U_{v}(t)-V^{*}(v)\leq U_{x}(t)-V^{*}(x)\leq\rho_{k}/2.

V∗​(u)≤Uu​(t)≤λ+ρk/2.V^{*}(u)\leq U_{u}(t)\leq\lambda+\rho_{k}/2.

V∗​(v)=maxu∈Ch⁡(v)⁡V∗​(u)≤λ+ρk/2.V^{*}(v)=\max_{u\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)}V^{*}(u)\leq\lambda+\rho_{k}/2.

V∗​(u)≥Lu​(t)≥λ−ρk/2.V^{*}(u)\geq L_{u}(t)\geq\lambda-\rho_{k}/2.
